wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.notes: Warm-up. The start is a two-bolt anchor on a short vertical wall in the middle of the granite apron. Wander up the easy slab a few metres right of Africa Flake until the angle steepens; gear placements plus a single bolt lead to the anchor.
First real friction: four bolts protect moves on small knobs, then one gear placement and a last bolt reach the anchor. Pure smearing and edging on sticky knobbed granite.

Follow a left-facing edge for about 10 m to a bolt guarding a diagonal dike crossing. Good knobs and four bolts lead across a rock bridge around a hole in the slab; one more bolt and some gear finish at the anchor.
Easy knobby ground past four bolts to a ledge on top of the feature to the right. There is no need to climb on the dirty feature itself.
The first bolt protects moves over a sill, then four more lead through big breadloaf knobs. Aim for a clean crack above, protect it with gear and follow it to the anchor.

Bolts protect the entry into a thin crack, very narrow at the bottom and widening as it rises; bring tiny nuts and cams (1/8 to 1/2 inch). From the top of the crack, two bolts lead left over a pair of overlaps; above the second overlap, go straight up a path through the bushes to the anchor.

Move the belay first: walk through the Bubba Compactor (a ledge behind a big detached flake), step down and contour to a thin ledge with a belay bolt, backed up with a 2-inch piece. Clip a bolt, protect the big flakes with gear, then two bolts on top of the flake guard the crux step up a thin dike. Four bolts on the slab above reach the anchor.
Six bolts of thin, sustained friction slab lead to a hole in the rock that takes gear from 1 to 3 inches for the belay.

Step right past a bush to find the first bolt. Smear up and across a right-facing edge, trend right along bolts, then continue up thin ground past more bolts. A 1-inch piece in an overlap crack leads to the anchor.

The most delicate slab: smearing on small knobs past eight bolts to a horizontal crack that takes a 2-inch cam, then two more bolts to a left-facing corner with a gear placement. The anchor sits on top of a pedestal.

Climb past a couple of right-facing corners on gear and clip two bolts to reach the Inverted Prow dihedral, which takes only very small cams. Follow the ramp beside it, then move up onto the buttress crest to a chain anchor.
Blocky, ledgy climbing up the right side of the buttress crest to an anchor on the crest.
Scramble up the ridge until trees force a move right. Step down onto the slab layer just under the trees and follow its dihedral, which protects well, to an anchor on a small stance.

Step right past a clean 3-inch crack and around the bulge up and right. Climb a rib with a horizontal crack that takes a 1/2-inch piece, then a bolt; past bushes, a white rib has one more bolt. Go left of a tree with an old sling and through wide cracks between blocks to the summit chain anchor.

wa_inspiration_peak_west_ridge.notes: Cross the bergschrund at the toe of the ridge and climb an approach gully until it makes sense to break out onto the ridge proper; loose, glacier-polished rock near the schrund.

Continue up compact slab low on the ridge to gain the crest; protection is sparse on this low-angle friction, and a 3-pin anchor here was rebuilt in June 2024 because natural gear placements are scarce.
Face climbing just right of the ridge crest on sustained, compact slab — the start of roughly 1,300 vertical feet of sustained 5.6/5.7 climbing that defines the lower route.
Continued sustained slab climbing on the lower ridge; holds are small and rounded, rewarding careful footwork over strength.
Slab and low-angle corners lead to a 2-pin anchor below a left-facing corner; rock quality is noticeably better here than down at the schrund.
Climb the left-facing corner directly; clean edges and a steady crack make this one of the better-protected pitches on the lower ridge.
Head up and right via a series of corners to a sloping ledge with a 2-pin anchor; sustained, technical corner climbing.

A large, obvious corner capped by a short chimney; awkward stemming and a step left onto slab make this the technical crux of the West Ridge, even though it's graded the same as several pitches below.
Slab climbing directly above the chimney corner, easing off slightly as the ridge crest broadens.
A rising, exposed traverse of about 100 feet across lichen-covered ledges to a small horn slung with cord for the belay; route-finding along the ledge system matters more than raw difficulty.
Climb back onto the ridge crest on markedly better rock than lower down — clean, solid gneiss typical of the upper mountain.
Roughly 200 feet of easy 5th-class scrambling along the crest to the base of the summit headwall; still roped given the exposure on both sides of the narrow ridge.
Climb the right side of the short, featured summit headwall to a horn-and-pin anchor; solid rock with good edges on a steep, exposed final move.
Pull through a rock-scar roof low on the pitch, then run out about 200 feet of lower-angle rock to the summit ridge — the last pitch of the climb, topping out just short of the true summit.
